provenance.curriculum_basis: NERDC Basic Science and Technology Curriculum, Primary 4, Basic Technology theme: Technology and You, Vehicles, Materials and Maintenance, and Basic Motor Vehicle Parts.
provenance.source_title: Basic Science and Technology Curriculum — Primary 4
provenance.source_note: NERDC specifies the Primary 4 Basic Technology topics and performance objectives but does not allocate them to First or Second Term. The term placement below is a proposed progression to cover NERDC topics not found in the supplied Third-Term Basic Technology export. It is not presented as an official state term scheme.
provenance.overlap_review: The proposed lessons focus on Vehicles, Materials and Maintenance, and Internal Motor Vehicle Parts. The supplied Third-Term source focuses on technology products, ICT gadgets, shape construction, buildings and energy; no exact lesson-title overlap is intended.

lessons.title: Vehicles: Meaning, Types and Uses
objectives: Explain the meaning of a vehicle.
Identify common types of vehicles.
State uses of vehicles in the community.
Give one disadvantage of using vehicles.
lessons.lesson: A vehicle is a means of transport used to carry people or goods from one place to another. Vehicles may travel on land, on water or in the air. Land vehicles include bicycles, motorcycles, cars, buses and trucks. Water vehicles include canoes, boats and ships. Air vehicles include aeroplanes and helicopters. Vehicles help people travel, carry farm produce and move goods to markets. Some vehicles use fuel and can cause air pollution, noise or traffic accidents when they are not used safely.
examples: A bicycle carries a person on land.
A boat carries people or goods on water.
A truck transports goods.
lessons.activity: Pupils classify pictures of vehicles into land, water and air groups and explain one use of each group.
evaluation: What is a vehicle?
Name three land vehicles.
Give two examples of water vehicles.
State two uses of vehicles.
Mention one disadvantage of vehicles.

lessons.title: External Parts of Vehicles and Their Functions
objectives: Identify common external parts of a motor vehicle.
State the functions of selected external parts.
Explain why vehicle parts should be in good condition.
lessons.lesson: External parts are parts of a vehicle that can be seen from outside. A vehicle may have tyres or wheels, doors, windows, lights, mirrors, a windscreen, a bonnet and a number plate. Wheels help the vehicle move. Headlights help the driver see at night and help others notice the vehicle. Mirrors help the driver observe what is behind and beside the vehicle. Doors allow people to enter and leave. Pupils should identify parts from pictures or a parked vehicle viewed with an adult; they must never stand in traffic or touch moving parts.
examples: Tyres help a car move along the road.
Headlights help drivers see in darkness.
Mirrors help drivers observe nearby traffic.
lessons.activity: Using a labelled picture or toy vehicle, pupils point to external parts and match each part to its function.
evaluation: Name five external parts of a motor vehicle.
What is the function of a tyre?
Why are headlights important?
What do mirrors help a driver do?

lessons.title: Uses and Disadvantages of Vehicles
objectives: Describe ways vehicles help people and communities.
Identify possible disadvantages of vehicles.
Suggest simple ways to reduce transport-related risks.
lessons.lesson: Vehicles help people travel to school, work, hospitals and markets. They also transport food, building materials and other goods. Ambulances help carry sick or injured people to hospitals, while fire engines help emergency workers. However, vehicles may cause traffic accidents, noise and air pollution. Poorly maintained vehicles can be unsafe. People can reduce risks by obeying traffic rules, using safe crossings, wearing seat belts in cars and keeping away from moving vehicles.
examples: A bus carries many passengers.
A truck moves goods to a market.
An ambulance transports a patient.
lessons.activity: Pupils match vehicle pictures to their uses and identify one safety rule for each situation.
evaluation: State three uses of vehicles.
Give two examples of vehicles used for emergencies.
Mention two disadvantages of vehicles.
State three ways to stay safe around vehicles.

lessons.title: Internal Parts of a Motor Vehicle and Their Functions
objectives: Identify selected internal parts of a motor vehicle from a diagram.
State the functions of seat belts, steering, brakes, pedals and gears.
Explain why vehicle safety features are important.
lessons.lesson: Internal parts are parts found inside a motor vehicle or within its passenger area. A steering wheel helps the driver control direction. Brakes help slow down or stop the vehicle. Pedals are operated by the driver to control movement. Gears help the engine and wheels work at suitable speeds. Seat belts help hold passengers safely in their seats during sudden stops. Some vehicles have airbags that provide additional protection in certain crashes. Pupils should learn from diagrams or a stationary vehicle with an adult; they must not operate a vehicle or touch its controls.
examples: The steering wheel helps control direction.
The brake helps stop the vehicle.
A seat belt helps protect passengers.
lessons.activity: Pupils label a teacher-provided motor-vehicle diagram and match each internal part to its function. No vehicle is started or operated.
evaluation: Name four internal parts of a motor vehicle.
What does the steering wheel do?
What is the function of a brake?
Why should passengers wear seat belts?

lessons.title: Materials Used in Technology
objectives: Identify wood, metal and plastic as materials used in technology.
Give examples of objects made from each material.
State one reason a material is chosen for a particular use.
lessons.lesson: Materials are substances used to make objects and products. Common materials used in technology include wood, metal and plastic. Wood comes from trees and is used for furniture, doors and some handles. Metal is used for tools, gates, vehicle bodies and cooking pots. Plastic is used for containers, buckets, toys and some electrical coverings. A material is selected because of its properties, such as strength, weight, flexibility or resistance to water. Not every material is suitable for every job.
examples: A wooden desk is made mainly from wood.
A cooking pot may be made from metal.
A water bucket may be made from plastic.
lessons.activity: Pupils examine safe sample objects and group them by material. They describe why the material may be suitable for the object's use.
evaluation: Name three materials used in technology.
Give two objects made from wood.
Give two objects made from metal.
Why is plastic used to make some buckets?

lessons.title: Types and Properties of Wood, Metal and Plastic
objectives: Describe simple properties of wood, metal and plastic.
Compare materials by strength, weight and flexibility.
Match materials to suitable everyday uses.
lessons.lesson: Different materials have different properties. Many metals are strong and can be shaped, but some metals may rust when exposed to water and air. Wood is useful for furniture and building parts, but it can be damaged by water or insects if not protected. Plastic is often light and can be shaped into many forms; some plastics can become weak when exposed to heat. The correct material should be chosen for the job. Pupils should handle only clean, safe samples provided by the teacher.
examples: Metal is used for some gates because it can be strong.
Wood is used for desks and chairs.
Plastic is used for light containers.
lessons.activity: Pupils compare safe samples of wood, metal and plastic by looking and touching. They record simple observations without using sharp tools or heating materials.
evaluation: State one property of metal.
Give one use of wood.
Why is plastic used for some containers?
Choose a suitable material for a school desk and explain why.

lessons.title: Maintenance: Meaning, Need and Importance
objectives: Explain the meaning of maintenance.
State reasons for maintaining tools, equipment and other products.
Identify simple maintenance activities.
lessons.lesson: Maintenance means taking care of an object or equipment so that it remains useful and safe. Maintenance may include cleaning, drying, checking for damage, tightening loose parts and storing items properly. Regular care can make tools and products last longer, reduce waste and help prevent accidents. Damaged electrical items, sharp tools and machines should be reported to an adult and should not be repaired by pupils.
examples: Wiping a clean tool dry after use helps prevent rust.
Keeping books and equipment in their proper places prevents damage.
Reporting a broken chair helps prevent injury.
lessons.activity: Pupils inspect pictures of well-maintained and poorly maintained objects and suggest safe care actions.
evaluation: What is maintenance?
Give three reasons for maintaining objects.
Name four simple maintenance activities.
What should a pupil do when an electrical item is damaged?

lessons.title: Caring for Materials, Tools and Technology Products
objectives: Describe safe ways to care for wood, metal and plastic products.
Identify suitable storage practices.
Explain why damaged tools and equipment must be reported.
lessons.lesson: Different materials need suitable care. Wooden objects should be kept reasonably dry and protected from damage. Metal objects should be cleaned and dried to reduce rust. Plastic objects should be kept away from excessive heat and should not be overloaded. Tools should be cleaned and stored in their proper places after use. Pupils must not sharpen blades, repair electrical equipment or operate power tools. Any damaged tool or product should be reported to a teacher or another responsible adult.
examples: Drying a metal tool after cleaning helps prevent rust.
Keeping plastic items away from fire prevents melting.
Storing tools in a safe place reduces accidents.
lessons.activity: Pupils prepare a simple care chart for one wooden object, one metal object and one plastic object found in school.
evaluation: How can metal objects be protected from rust?
Why should plastic be kept away from fire?
State three safe storage practices.
What should pupils do with damaged tools?
